summary: Defines a format for bibliographic records that describe technical reports. It is intended for exchanging catalogue-style information about reports, and is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1807 defines a plain-text format for bibliographic records: the catalogue entries that describe a technical report. Every value in a record is preceded by a short alphabetic tag and two colons, so a person can read the record and a program can pick out the parts it needs. The format lets organisations announce new reports by email or file transfer instead of by post.

subtitle: A plain-text, tag-based record format for announcing technical reports by email or file transfer instead of by post.

tldr.problem: Universities and research organisations announced new technical reports by posting bibliographic records through the postal services, which cost money, arrived late and could not be filed electronically.
tldr.mechanism: Each record is plain text in which every value is preceded by an alphabetic tag and two colons, with four mandatory fields, a set of optional ones, and rules for line length, continuation and character set.
tldr.outcome: The format let reports be announced by email or file transfer and could be read or written with any text editor, and it became the interchange format of the Dienst and SIFT bibliographic systems.

today: RFC 1807 is an Informational memo published in June 1995. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it revises RFC 1357 with new fields for handles, other access points, keywords and withdrawal.

sections.title: Why a Machine-Readable Record
sections.content:
Many universities and other research and development organisations routinely announce new technical reports by mailing, through the postal services, the bibliographic records of those reports. Those mailings have non-trivial cost and delay, and their recipients cannot conveniently file them electronically for later retrieval and searches.

Publishing organisations that wish to use email or file transfer to obtain these announcements can do so by using the format in this memo. Organisations may automate to any degree, or not at all, both the creation of records about their own publications and the handling of records received from other organisations.

The format is designed to be simple, for people and for machines, to be easy to read and to create without any special programs. It is a tagged format with self-explaining alphabetic tags, so that records can be prepared and read with any text editor. The memo defines the format of the records, not how to process them.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo replaces postal announcements of new technical reports with records sent by email or file transfer. Each record is plain text with a tag in front of every value, so a person can read it and a program can pick out the parts it needs.

sections.title: The Fields of a Record
sections.content:
A record contains several fields. Each field starts with its tag, also called the field ID, which is a reserved identifier containing no separators, at the beginning of a new line with or without spaces before it. The tag is followed by two colons and then the field data.

Three fields are mandatory, and a record without them is invalid: BIB-VERSION, which identifies the version of the format used to create the record, ID, which identifies the record and is used in managing it, and ENTRY, the date the record was created. A fourth mandatory field, END, must be the last entry of a record and repeats the ID. The remaining fields are optional: ORGANIZATION, TITLE, TYPE, REVISION, WITHDRAW, AUTHOR, CORP-AUTHOR, CONTACT, DATE, PAGES, COPYRIGHT, HANDLE, OTHER_ACCESS, RETRIEVAL, KEYWORD, CR-CATEGORY, PERIOD, SERIES, MONITORING, FUNDING, CONTRACT, GRANT, LANGUAGE, NOTES and ABSTRACT.

All fields, unless specifically not permitted to, may appear in any order and may be repeated as needed, for example the AUTHOR field, and the order of repeated fields is always preserved. The CR-CATEGORY field, the Computer Reviews Category index for computer science publications, is included, and the memo expects similar fields to be added for other domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Every record has a version tag, an identifier, the date it was created, and an end tag that repeats the identifier. Everything else, from the title and authors to the keywords and the abstract, is optional, and any field can appear more than once.

sections.title: Tags, Colons and Continuation Lines
sections.content:
Lines are limited to 79 characters. When needed, fields may continue over several lines with an implied space in between, and to simplify use no special marking shows that a line continues. A field is therefore terminated by a line that starts, apart from white space, with a word followed by two colons. The END:: field is terminated by the end of the line. For improved human readability, continuation lines are suggested to start with some spaces.

Only printable ASCII characters are to be used. The permissible characters are ASCII codes 040 (Space) through 176 (~), and line breaks which are \012 (LF) or \012\015 (CRLF). Empty lines indicate a paragraph break, and a tab, code \009, must be replaced by spaces. Tabs, null characters, DEL and backspaces make the record invalid.

Full 8-bit ASCII may be used, but the memo warns that some electronic mailers cannot handle 8-bit ASCII, so such records may need to be transported by other mechanisms. Throughout the memo the word publisher means the publishing organisation of a report, such as a university or one of its departments, not necessarily an organisation authorised to issue ISBN numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Long values are written over several lines and the reader puts a space between them, because nothing marks the join. A line ends a field only when it starts with a tag. Only printable characters are allowed, and a tab has to be typed as spaces.

sections.title: Field Formats and Ordering
sections.content:
The BIB-VERSION field is the first field of any record and, in this version of the format, is always BIB-VERSION:: CS-TR-v2.1. A version that starts with the letter X, in either case, is considered experimental, and records sent with such a version should not be incorporated in the permanent database of the recipient.

The ID field has the form ID:: XXX//YYY, where XXX is the publisher ID, the controlled symbol of the publisher, and YYY is the ID of the publication as assigned by the publisher, such as the report number. That ID is typically printed on the cover and may contain slashes. The symbols DUMMY and TEST, in either case, are reserved for test records that should not be incorporated in the permanent database of the recipients.

The ENTRY field holds the date the record was created, written as Month Day, Year, with the month spelled out, a one or two digit day and a four digit year. The DATE field, the publication date, accepts Month Year or Month Day, Year. The REVISION field says the record is a revision of a previously issued one and is intended to replace it; it holds a date, optionally followed by a semicolon and free text describing the revision, and the revised record must be a complete record rather than a list of changes. If revision is omitted, the record is assumed to be a new record.

A WITHDRAW field means the document is no longer available, and should give the reason in free text; a withdraw record has all of the mandatory fields plus the withdraw field and a mandatory revision field. It is up to each institution to decide whether to delete the record or remove some of its fields. The HANDLE field is mandatory whenever the technical report is available in electronic form, and gives the permanent identifier used to retrieve the location of the data.
sections.plainLanguage: The version tag tells a reader which version of the format was used, and an experimental version is not to be filed. The identifier combines a publisher code with the report number, usually printed on the cover. A revision field says that a newer, complete record replaces an earlier one, and a withdraw field says the document is no longer available.

sections.title: A Worked Example Record
sections.content:
The memo gives a complete example record for a report from Oceanview University. It starts with the version, identifier and entry date, then gives the organization, the type, a revision date and its reason, the title, two authors with their contact details, the publication date, the page count, a copyright statement, a handle, two other access points, a retrieval note, a keyword, two Computer Reviews categories, a series, the funding and monitoring organizations, a contract number, the language, notes and the abstract. It ends with END:: repeating the identifier. The memo notes that the example has about 1,689 characters, 184 words, including about 249 characters, 36 words, in the abstract.

The abstract is highly recommended but not mandatory. Even though no limit is defined for its length, the memo suggests that applications should not be expected to handle more than 10,000 characters of it. The abstract is expected to be used for subject searching, since titles are not enough, and an English abstract is preferable even when the report is written in another language.

The memo also suggests that publishing organisations register their publisher ID symbols with IANA, in a way similar to the registration of other key names in the Internet, and that the producers of records always use the same name, exactly, in the ORGANIZATION field, so that received records can be handled automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows a complete record for a fictional report, including two authors, a copyright statement, a handle, two ways to reach the full text and an abstract. The abstract is the field a library searches, so it is worth including even though it is optional.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section of the memo says only this: security issues are not discussed in it. Elsewhere the memo notes that it places no limitations on the dissemination of the bibliographic records themselves, and that if there are limitations on the dissemination of the publication, they should be protected by some means such as passwords, which this format does not address.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security. It says the records themselves may be passed around freely, and that any restriction on the publication should be enforced by other means, such as a password.

viz.caption: THE FOUR MANDATORY FIELDS OF A BIBLIOGRAPHIC RECORD

items.label: FIRST FIELD
items.desc: The version of the format used to create the record.

items.label: SECOND FIELD
items.desc: Identifies the record: publisher symbol, then //, then the publication ID.

items.label: THIRD FIELD
items.desc: The date the record was created.

items.label: LAST FIELD
items.desc: Repeats the ID of the record it ends.

viz.caption: RULES FOR WRITING THE TEXT OF A RECORD

items.title: Tag first
items.text: Each field starts with its tag at the beginning of a line, then two colons, then the data.

items.title: Continuation lines
items.text: A long field runs over several lines with an implied space; the next tag ends the field.

items.title: Character set
items.text: Only printable ASCII, codes 040 to 176; a tab must be replaced by spaces.

items.title: Empty lines
items.text: An empty line marks a paragraph break, as in the abstract.

references.text: Cohen, D., ISI, RFC 1357, the original version of this format, July 1992.
